item.title: Tested & Ranked: The Best AI Image Generator Pakistan Options for Real Design Work
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Let's be completely real for a moment. Freelance groups on Facebook were filled with posts saying, “Humari field khatam ho gayi” (Our field is over).

But at my agency, Media Initiation, we looked at it differently. We saw it as a way to stop spending hours hunting for the perfect royalty-free stock image on Freepik or Shutterstock—only to find out that another local brand had already used the exact same image on their billboard.

Over the last year, I have personally tested almost every major AI image generator Pakistan has access to. I've used them for real client projects, from designing packaging for local startups to creating social media grids for real estate clients in Islamabad.

If you are a Pakistani designer looking to add AI to your workflow without losing the “human touch” that clients actually pay for, this honest, unfiltered review is for you.

The Reality Check: Why International Tutorials Don't Always Work for Us

If you watch a Western tech YouTuber, they will show you how to generate a flawless, ultra-realistic image of a futuristic sci-fi city or a cyberpunk coffee shop. That's great for entertainment, but it doesn't help you when a local client comes to you and says:

“Mujhe apni brand ke liye ek Pakistani family chahiye jo Eid ke kapre pehan kar smile kar rahi ho.” (I need a Pakistani family wearing Eid clothes and smiling for my brand).

This is where most mainstream AI tools fall flat. They don't understand our culture, our traditional clothing (Shalwar Kameez), or our facial features. When you type “Pakistani man,” many tools mistakenly output images that look like generic Middle Eastern models or add strange, inaccurate cultural items.

To save you from wasting your internet data and time, I've broken down which platforms actually get our local context right.

1. Midjourney: The King of Cinematic Visuals (But with a Catch)

If you want absolute jaw-dropping visual quality, Midjourney is still the undisputed champion in 2026.

My Real-World Use Case

We were designing a concept poster for a premium local clothing brand. They wanted a background that looked like an ancient, rustic Haveli in Lahore, bathed in moody evening light. Finding a stock photo like that with the right lighting is nearly impossible.

The Prompt I Used: A cinematic wide shot of an ancient Lahori Haveli courtyard, brick walls, traditional arches, soft golden hour sunlight, hyper-realistic, shot on 35mm lens –ar 16:9 The Result: It gave me four options that looked like high-budget movie sets. I picked the best one, brought it into Adobe Photoshop, cut out our local model, and blended her into the scene.

Is Midjourney the Best AI Image Generator Pakistan Creative Teams Can Use?

Yes, for art direction, it is unmatched. However, it has two major drawbacks for Pakistani freelancers:

- No Free Tier: It requires a paid subscription, and paying in US Dollars from Pakistan right now, with international transactions and taxes, can feel quite heavy on a freelancer's wallet.

- The Discord Interface: It doesn't have a standard standalone app interface; you have to run it through Discord, which can feel incredibly confusing if you're just starting out.

2. Adobe Firefly: The Professional's Safest Choice

If you are already paying for an Adobe Creative Cloud subscription on your laptop or PC, Adobe Firefly is integrated right inside your Photoshop and Illustrator panels.

Why Firefly Wins on Commercial Projects

The biggest issue with most AI image generators in Pakistan is copyright. If you use a tool that scraped random art from Pinterest to train its AI, your client could technically face legal issues later if they use that asset in a major commercial product.

Adobe Firefly is trained exclusively on licensed images and public domain content.

- Generative Fill: I use this daily. If I have a great photo of a product but the background is a messy local market, I can select the background in Photoshop, type “clean white minimalist kitchen counter with marble texture,” and Firefly replaces it seamlessly while matching the original product's lighting.

3. Stable Diffusion (Focus / Automatic): The Free, Power-User Route

If you have a decent gaming PC or laptop (something with an Nvidia RTX card like a 3060 or 4060) and want a completely free AI image-generation workflow in Pakistan, Stable Diffusion is our best friend.

How to Build Local Assets Using Stable Diffusion

Unlike Midjourney, you can download Stable Diffusion models directly onto your local storage device and run them completely offline without paying a single Rupee.

- The “LoRA” Trick: The secret to making Stable Diffusion work for the Pakistani market is using specific community-made add-ons called LoRAs. You can go to open-source sites like Civitai and find models trained on South Asian, particularly Pakistani, truck art or local street aesthetics.

- Step-by-Step Prompting: When I need an authentic look, I structure my prompts using clear weights: A close-up portrait of a Pakistani woman in her late 20s, wearing an intricately embroidered dark green shalwar kameez, standing in a bright minimalist room, highly detailed skin texture, photorealistic, 8k resolution.

My Biggest AI Mistakes (And How to Avoid Them in AI Image Generator Pakistan)

- The “Six Fingers” Nightmare: AI still struggles with human anatomy. I once sent an automated layout to a client for a social media post, only to have them message back pointing out that the model in the image had six fingers on her left hand. Always zoom in on the eyes, teeth, and hands when showing a design to a client.

- Text Generation Failures: Don't try to generate text using AI images. If you need a signboard background that says signboardstro,” the AI will usually write something garbled like “Lhoare Bstiro.” Generate a clean background without text, then use Adobe Illustrator to add clean, vectorized typography on top.…

item.title: PageSift 1.7 "Resolve": Stop Trusting Retrieved Text — Verify the Conclusion
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

PageSift is a Rust web-content engine for LLM pipelines (305 stars, Apache-2.0). Version 1.7, released today, adds the layer that was still missing — checking the conclusions you draw from that text.

The problem: nobody verifies the answer

A retrieval pipeline hands text to a model. The model states conclusions: "the price is $42 a year", "it ships in March", "this tool causes fewer support tickets". Those sentences go into answers, reports, and databases. Nobody checks them.

And they rot. The price changes next month. Two sources disagree and the pipeline keeps whichever it read last. A press release gets copied by five sites and starts to look like five independent confirmations. A study that found a correlation gets quoted as proof of causation. Last year's price gets repeated as today's.

Scraping got the text back. Context (1.6) made the text traceable. The conclusion drawn from it was still taken on faith. Resolve is the layer that checks it.

One scenario, end to end

Say you monitor a product's price. The vendor's page says Widget Pro costs $42 per year. A reseller lists the same product at $45 per year. Your pipeline produces the sentence "Widget Pro costs $42 per year" and you ask Resolve to check it against the stored evidence.

The verdict is conflicted. Resolve tracks support and refutation as separate facts instead of averaging them into a score: one independent source supports the sentence, another independent source refutes it, and the record says exactly that, with citations to both.

Two weeks later the vendor raises the price to $50. The stored conclusion is not left standing. When the underlying evidence changes, Resolve re-checks only the conclusions that depend on the changed passages — and this one flips to refuted, with its full revision history preserved. A conclusion in Resolve is not a one-time judgment. It is a maintained object that stays answerable to its evidence.

The four ideas

1. A conclusion is a stored, versioned record. Each checked answer becomes a ConclusionRecord with one of nine states — supported, supported with qualifiers, refuted, conflicted, insufficient, temporal mismatch, causally unidentifiable, needs human review, observation degraded. Two of those states deserve emphasis: insufficient ("the evidence does not settle this") and causally unidentifiable ("the evidence shows correlation, not causation"). The system is allowed to say it cannot tell, and it does.

2. Checking is deterministic, in seven layers. The checker anchors every claim to its subject, so one product's price can never "confirm" another's. It keeps two time axes apart: when a page was observed versus the period the fact is valid for — a 2024 price cannot confirm a claim about today. It normalizes quantities, currencies, and billing periods, so $42 per month does not confirm $42 per year. It guards negation and dropped qualifiers ("does not include shipping" refutes "includes shipping"; an omitted "unless" downgrades a claim to qualified instead of supported). It refuses causal language on correlational evidence. It collapses copied sources that share one origin, so a syndicated reprint counts once, not five times. And it verifies that every citation actually reaches the passage it claims to support.

3. It argues against itself. After a check, Resolve runs a counter-search: it actively looks for errata, exceptions, and contradicting records that would overturn the conclusion, and attaches an audit of what it searched. The audit states its own limit in plain terms — in an open world, finding no counter-evidence is not proof. Absence of evidence is recorded as absence, never converted into confidence.

4. Conclusions are maintained, not just made. When sources change, an incremental reconciliation finds the affected conclusions and re-verifies only those, cutting off early when a change is a pure relocation or a reconfirmation. In the release evaluation this ran 4.47× faster than full re-verification — which is what makes it practical to re-check every stored conclusion every time its evidence moves, instead of auditing samples once in a while.

What the evaluation says

The release ships an adversarial evaluation set of 64 cases built to fool a checker: mirror copies, stale prices, billing-period swaps, negation traps, causal overreach. A keyword-overlap baseline — "the words appear in the source, so the claim is supported" — produced a false-support rate of 0.8333. It blessed five out of six wrong answers. Resolve's false-support rate on the same set was 0.0000, with supported precision and recall both at 1.0. In the mirror test, naive source counting gave false support at a rate of 1.0; after origin collapse, 0.

The core check runs at 9,448 checks per second (p50 96µs) on the benchmark machine. That number matters for one reason: verification this cheap does not have to be a nightly audit. It can run on every answer, at the moment the answer is produced.

One honest limitation, from the same evaluation: in deterministic mode, Resolve abstains on heavily metaphorical paraphrases — 3 out of 3 cases came back insufficient, with zero false supports. It would rather say "cannot tell" than guess at what a metaphor means. An optional hybrid mode lets a configured LLM judge those leftovers, but only with verbatim quote grounding, and it can never override a deterministic refutation.

When to use it, when not to

Use Resolve when a conclusion has to stay true: price and spec monitoring, answer auditing for RAG and agent systems, research claims you keep citing, any pipeline where a wrong sentence costs more than the check does.…

item.title: Razorpay Payment Successful but WooCommerce Order Pending
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

A customer paid, Razorpay shows the money, and your WooCommerce order still says "Pending payment" or never appeared. The usual cause is not the payment: it is that your store never received, or rejected, Razorpay's server notification (the webhook) that says the payment succeeded. Work through the checks below in order. Most stores find the cause in the first three.

Do not refund automatically and do not ask the customer to pay again until you have checked the payment status in Razorpay.

Why this happens

When a customer pays, two separate messages travel. The first goes through the customer's browser: after payment, the checkout page sends the payment result back to your store. If the customer closes the tab, loses signal or is switched to another app (common with UPI), that message never arrives. The second goes directly from Razorpay's servers to your store: the webhook. Razorpay's documentation describes webhooks as server-to-server notifications sent asynchronously when events occur, such as payment.authorized or order.paid (Razorpay webhooks). It also says that capturing payments for which you did not get a response on the client side is "perhaps the most important use case" for the payment.authorized event. If the browser message fails and the webhook also fails, the order stays pending.

Step 1: check the payment status in Razorpay

Open the payment in your Razorpay dashboard and note its status.

- Captured. The money is yours, and the problem is on your store side. Continue to step 2.

- Authorized, not captured. The bank approved it but the payment has not been captured. Razorpay states that payments in the authorized state must be captured within 3 days of creation, and that payments not captured within that period are refunded automatically to the customer (payment capture settings). Check your capture setting in the dashboard. Only the Razorpay account owner can change it.

- Late authorization. Razorpay's docs explain that when the bank's status does not reach Razorpay immediately, it polls for up to 3 days, so a payment shown as failed can later become authorized. Do not cancel the order in the first hours.

- Failed. The customer was not charged. If they report a debit, ask them to wait for the bank's automatic reversal and share the bank reference.

Step 2: read the WooCommerce order notes

Open the order and read the notes on the right. Look for lines about the Razorpay payment ID, a signature check or a cancellation. The note "Unpaid order cancelled - time limit reached." means WooCommerce's own unpaid-order timer cancelled the order, which is a different problem: see WooCommerce orders cancelled automatically.

Step 3: check that the webhook exists and points to your store

In the Razorpay dashboard, open Webhooks. You need an active webhook that points at your current store address. For the official Razorpay WooCommerce plugin, the webhook address is your site's admin-post.php address with ?action=rzp_wc_webhook added, as set in the plugin's code; the plugin can create the webhook for you when you save its settings. Check that:

- the address uses your live domain, with the right https:// and www form, with no leftover staging domain;

- the events include payment.authorized (and ideally order.paid and payment.failed);

- the webhook is active, not disabled.

If you changed your domain recently, the old webhook may still point to the old one.

Step 4: check the webhook secret

Razorpay signs each webhook with your secret, and the signature arrives in the X-Razorpay-Signature header. Razorpay says the signature is calculated with HMAC SHA256, using the webhook secret as the key and the raw request body as the message (validate and test webhooks). If the secret in your Razorpay webhook settings differs from the secret saved in the WooCommerce plugin settings, every webhook fails verification, and the order is never updated. Razorpay also notes that if you change the webhook secret, retries of older events must be validated with the old secret, because the new one causes a mismatch. Re-save the same secret in both places.

Step 5: look for something blocking Razorpay

Razorpay's request is an HTTP POST from outside your site. These commonly block it:

- a firewall or security plugin (including your host's firewall or Cloudflare rules) blocking unknown POST requests to admin-post.php;

- a maintenance-mode or "coming soon" plugin returning a page instead of the store;

- password protection (HTTP authentication) on the site or on a staging copy;

- a redirect from http:// to https:// or between www and non-www. A redirect can drop the POST body, so use the final address in the webhook.

Check your host's firewall log and your security plugin's blocked-requests log for requests from Razorpay around the payment time.

Step 6: allow time, and check WordPress cron

The plugin's code logs that it handles the payment.authorized event "by cron", and its changelog for version 3.9.4 says "Added delay of 5 minutes to webhook process". So a short delay before the order updates can be normal. If orders stay pending long after that, confirm that WordPress scheduled tasks run. If DISABLE_WP_CRON is set in your configuration, a real server cron job must call wp-cron.php. You can check your plugin version in the plugins list, as behaviour changes between versions.

Step 7: test the webhook

Razorpay lets you test webhooks in test mode: you can set up a webhook, trigger test events from a test transaction and check whether your endpoint receives them (validate and test webhooks). Run one test payment on your staging copy or in test mode and watch the order notes.

Step 8: fix the orders that are already stuck

For each affected order:

- Confirm in the Razorpay dashboard that the payment is captured for the right amount and matches the order.

- If it is captured, change the order to Processing (or Completed for digital goods), and add a note with the Razorpay payment ID.…

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-23 06:30 UTC

item.title: Yes, 17M lines of Lean is a lot
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Yes, 17m lines of Lean is a lot

The recent proof of the Riemann hypothesis came with a statistic attached: the proof is 17 million lines of Lean. Beyond the philosophical questions of what it means to have a proof longer than any human could comprehend, I’m left with a simpler question: is that as large as it sounds?

To investigate, I hunted for collections of Lean proofs online. I found two and charted the lengths of their proofs.

(All charts have a log x axis, which makes 17m lines look a lot closer to 1m and 100k than it really is.)

Famous theorems in Mathlib

Mathlib maintains a collection of famous proofs. There are over 1k but only 259 have Lean associated, which I chart here.

These are all human generated, and as we can see, they come nowhere close to 17m.

Every Lean package on Reservoir

Reservoir indexes every published Lean package, 938 of which have Lean code on GitHub. This one has a lot more data, including AI assisted proofs. We even have a few that are over 16m!:

- 88m: Qiuzhen-CFSG/CFSG this appears to be an AI built proof that is still a work in progress.

- 36m: CBirkbeck/LeanBridge, a project linking the LMFDB database of number theory objects to Mathlib. This isn’t really a proof: about 98% of its Lean is files generated by scripts that check the database’s numbers one by one. The hand-written part is closer to 500k lines.

- 27m: anthropics/fermats-last-theorem is another Anthropic special: a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, published on GitHub in September. Its README says “the Lean sources were produced by AI agents building on human-written open-source Lean”, including the human FLT project led by Kevin Buzzard, which is about 60k lines and still in progress. The AI version is roughly 450 times longer.

So yes, 17m lines is a lot.

Source: Hacker News | Published: 2026-11-23 05:00 UTC

item.title: A Partial Evaluator for C
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Tempo is an off-line specializer; it is divided into two phases: analysis and specialization.

- The input to the analysis phase consists of a program and a description

of which inputs will be known during specialization and which will be unknown.

Based on this knowledge, dependency analyses propagate information about

known and unknown values throughout the code and produce an annotated program,

indicating how each program construct should be transformed during specialization.

Because C is an imperative language including pointers, the analysis phase

performs alias and side-effect analyses in addition to binding-time

analyses. The accuracy of these analyses is targeted towards keeping

track of known values across procedures, data structures, and pointers.

Following the analysis phase, the specialization phase generates a specialized program based on the annotated program and the values of the known inputs. Tempo can specialize programs at compile time (i.e., source-to-source tranformation) as well as run time (i.e., run-time binary code generation).

miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[])

{

int i = 0;

while( *fmt != '\0' ) {

if( *fmt != '%' )

putchar(*fmt);

else

switch(*++fmt) {

case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;

case '%' : putchar('%');     break;

default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;

}

fmt++;

}

}

/*  LEGEND:  STATIC  DYNAMIC

*/

miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[])

{

int i = 0;

while( *fmt != '\0' ) {

if( *fmt != '%' )

putchar(*fmt);

else

switch(*++fmt) {

case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;

case '%' : putchar('%');     break;

default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;

}

fmt++;

}

}

The visualization of the analysis is very important for the user to

assess the amount of specialization in the code. Furthermore, the analysis

speeds up the specialization process (as opposed to

on-line partial

evaluators). The analysis is inter-procedural and takes into account pointer

aliases and side-effects.

miniprintf_1(int val[])

{

putchar( '<'    );

putint ( val[0] );

putchar( ','    );

putint ( val[1] );

putchar( '>'    );

}

/*

* Some dynamic execution context for variable 'format'

*/

spec_printf = rts_miniprintf_1(format);

...

(*spec_printf)(val1);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val1) */

(*spec_printf)(val2);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val2) */

- Operating system and networking:

- Sun RPC, Chorus IPC, BSD packet filter, Unix signals, active networks,

- Computer graphics (various filtering algorithms),

- Scientific computation (trajectory, FFT, math libraries),

- Software architectures and mechanisms:

- Domain specific languages GAL, PLAN-P),

- Selective broadcast (implicit invocation),

- Pattern matching,

- Interpreters,

- Software layers,

- Generic libraries.

Besides C, Tempo is currently being used as a back-end for specializing

Java programs using Harissa, a JavaVM-to-C compiler.

Fortran and C++ programs have also been specialized using translators to

C.

- Cyclone

- Cyclone is a mobile code system being developed as part of the SwitchWare active-network project at the University of Pennsylvania. Cyclone uses two ideas to make mobile code safe as well as fast: run-time code generation and proof-carrying code. Cyclone relies on Tempo's analysis front-end (i.e. the binding-time analysis) and on TAL/T, an extension of the TAL typed assembly language.

Depending on request, if the distribution

of Tempo is a success, we might organize another workshop later. It would

less be like a ``winter school'' but rather like a real workshop with users

presenting applications and open discussions about possible improvements.

It would be preceded by an optional one-day tutorial for people not knowing

partial evaluation or Tempo.

Getting access to Tempo no longer requires signing a license agreement. Tempo is simply available via anonymous FTP, as described below. In any case, we would very much like to hear from you if you are an active Tempo user. If you are, please also let us know if and for what purpose you are using Tempo, by sending an email to tempo@labri.fr. We will by default add you to our tempo talk mailing list tempo-talk@labri.fr, where future Tempo releases will be announced, and Tempo users can discuss practical problems using Tempo.

In case of any problem with getting or installing the distribution,

item.title: Kodak’s next collectible is a tiny digital photo frame that doubles as a tracker
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

After expanding its Charmera collection with a Millennium Edition featuring Y2K-inspired designs earlier this year, Reto’s follow-up to its tiny Kodak camera is an equally small digital photo frame you can use to display your shots. But while the Charmera’s usefulness stopped at snapping grainy photos and terrible videos, the Kodak SlideTag goes one step further. It also functions as a Bluetooth tracker that’s compatible with either Apple’s Find My or Google’s Find Hub tracking networks.

Kodak’s next collectible is a tiny digital photo frame that doubles as a tracker

You can personalize the SlideTag with a photo slideshow, message, or QR code transferred from your phone over Bluetooth.

The Kodak SlideTag will be available for $34.99 each and, like the Charmera, will feature a series of retro designs distributed in mystery boxes so you don’t know which one you’re going to get. Kodak also sells a complete set of all eight vintage designs for $279.92 if you don’t like mysteries; however, there’s a ninth “secret edition” only available in the individual boxes with a sleek metallic finish.

For those who grew up in an era where projectors are small enough to integrate into phones, the SlideTag is designed to look like a modernized version of the film slides that were used to project photos decades ago. Instead of film, the SlideTag features a 1.54-inch color E Ink screen that mixes six colored inks to display photos at a resolution of 240 x 240.

The color reproduction won’t be as accurate as an LCD or OLED screen, but the SlideTag can hold and cycle up to 12 photos transferred to the device over Bluetooth from Kodak’s Memory Link app running on a mobile device. You can also use it to display a short to-do list, contact details, a countdown timer, or a QR code linking to wherever you want.

As a tracker it’s not quite as functional as an Apple AirTag or Google’s Pixel Tag, which use features like ultra wideband (UWB) and Channel Sounding to make them easier to find. The SlideTag sticks to basic Bluetooth with a range of up to 30 meters out in the open and a 75-decibel buzzer to help locate it when you’re close. Battery life will vary depending on how frequently you use tracking features or refresh the displayed image, but the SlideTag uses a common CR2032 coin cell battery that’s easy to replace.

item.title: Here's how much Starlink cost in 2020 vs. 2026
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Here's how much Starlink cost in 2020 vs. 2026

Starlink's cheapest home plan costs $44 less per month than it did in 2020, but hardware ownership and regional pricing have changed.

Starlink rolled out its public beta in October 2020, with the equipment costing $499 and the monthly subscription $99. Six years down the road, SpaceX's satellite internet service starts at $55 monthly for US customers, with equipment rentals available at no upfront cost in select areas. That's $44 less a month, or $528 less annually, on the subscription cost alone.

Unlike today's renters, those early-bird beta subscribers owned the equipment they paid for, but they were also asked to expect occasional outages, making that initial cost of nearly $600 a pretty sizable commitment. Today, Starlink offers three separate residential tiers at different network speeds and price plans.

The company also jacked up its residential rates in 2026, but the entry-level rate is still lower than it was in 2020. Throw in discounts and fluctuating rates based on local demand, and two customers could end up paying vastly different bills for the same satellite internet service.

In 2020, $598 got you into the 'Better Than Nothing Beta'

SpaceX's first public beta was rolled out as the "Better Than Nothing Beta." True to its very transparent (and accurate) name, customers were asked to expect download speeds of 50 to 150 Mbps and latency of 20 to 40ms, paired with occasional periods of zero connectivity.

The hardware kit with the price tag of $499 included Starlink's original circular satellite dish, a mounting tripod and a Wi-Fi router. With the first $99 monthly subscription payment, the initial cost came to $598, excluding shipping and taxes. So if the monthly rate remained the same, the first year's total would've been $1,687, including the equipment.

What customers with reliable broadband might scoff at, though, could still be an acceptable price for those stuck with slow DSL or unreliable cellular service, even with occasional outages.

SpaceX did hike the monthly rates to $110 back in March 2022, and it took effect for current users in April 2022. The hardware cost also went up to $599 for new users and $549 for customers with existing deposits. The culprit, according to the company, was inflation. In 2023, there were two prices for residential subscriptions: $90 in areas where there was excess network capacity and $120 in areas where there was limited network capacity.

In 2026, $55 a month doesn't buy you the dish

The satellite internet service is now available with three primary residential plans: Residential 100 Mbps for $55 per month, Residential 200 Mbps for $85 and Residential Max at $130. Each plan offers unlimited data, but the first two are locked to speed limits. The Max plan does get higher network priority and claims speeds of 400 Mbps or higher in suitable conditions.

In May 2026, SpaceX hiked those prices by $5, $5 and $10, respectively. In October 2026, additional location-based changes were announced, with some Residential Max customers told their bills would rise to $156 per month while others were told their bills would fall. PCMag reported that some new subscribers scored up to 50 percent off in a promotion running through November 30, 2026. Starlink said certain discounts last as long as the subscription remains active.

Shelling out hundreds of dollars upfront for a dish isn't the only option anymore. Starlink is now offering equipment rentals in several regions, and while Ars Technica confirmed that the company introduced a $10 monthly rental fee in June 2026, the fee was reportedly waived for some new orders in July 2026. Starlink still owns the rented hardware, and subscribers need to return the full kit within 30 days of canceling their plan or pay its retail price.

Subscribers already enjoying limited-time promotional rates keep their discounts until their offers expire. Regional pricing applies afterward, and changing plans during a promotion can also end the discount.

Starlink can be more expensive than cable, fiber or 5G home internet, but availability is where the value lies. The company's portable Roam service is available at $55 for 100GB of high-speed internet, after which speeds go down. If you don't want the high-speed data cap, Roam Unlimited costs $175 per month.

item.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.

But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year.

“We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch.

Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said.

Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.

Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win.

Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation.

“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials.

Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch.

After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.

“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations.
